narrative:
The model predicted a 72% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 2.60, it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted. Next, your family's upper-middle income bracket added further weight toward rejection; while this is the most common income group among accepted students (45%), the model still interpreted it as increasing risk in your overall profile. Finally, your first-year law school decile ranking of 7 also contributed to the negative outlook, though it was the least influential of the three. Interestingly, this decile is actually higher than the average of accepted students (6.0), yet it was not enough to offset the other signals.

Taken together, these elements led the model to conclude you were more likely to struggle with the bar exam than to pass it. 

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in the remaining years of law school and consider targeted bar-prep resources that have helped students with similar profiles succeed on their second attempt. Strengthening those areas could meaningfully change future predictions. (218 words)
